tasks.task_description: Build a statistical model of Olympic country medal counts (gold and total) from the provided datasets only, with uncertainty estimates, and validate it out-of-sample.
tasks.task_analysis: Two sources with a hard alignment problem: (1) summerOly_medal_counts.csv gives official country-level gold/silver/bronze/total per Games (source of truth, 1,435 rows, 1896-2024); (2) summerOly_athletes.csv gives athlete-level rows with a 3-letter NOC code that does NOT consistently match the country names in the medal table (e.g. CHN rows are not China's official 2024 medals, some codes blank; China/Japan/Australia/Brazil/Netherlands/Germany have no 2024 rows at all). Repairs: programs.csv read as cp1252 (UTF-8 fails; 0x95 byte = bullet); 1,466 fully duplicated athlete rows dropped; hosts.csv BOM/leading-space/parenthetical cleaned, cancelled years dropped; code->name mapping by unique (gold,silver,bronze) tally per Games year plus a manual map for renamed entities (URS/EUN/ROC, GDR/FRG, YUG/SCG, TPE, ANZ, AHO, BOH, UAR, SIN, WIF). Rows whose code cannot be tied to exactly one official country row are excluded from athlete-derived features but never alter official counts. Data repairs are documented in code/clean.py and results/tables/. Assumptions: official counts are correct; the athlete file's sport split is used only where its mapped total covers >=60% of the official country-year total, otherwise the country-year is carried by a residual 'Other' sport row so every official total is fully represented.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Two complementary layers, both fitted by maximum likelihood (L-BFGS on a sparse design matrix, log link).
(1) Poisson GLM panel (code/model.py): log lambda_{c,s,t} = a_c + b_s + g_t + h*H_{c,t} + d_p*P_{c,t} + d_a*log1p(Par_{c,t}), Y ~ Poisson(lambda), with country effect a_c, sport effect b_s (event scarcity), Games-year effect g_t (program size/era), host indicator H, post-host indicator P (hosted within the previous two Games), and log-participation. This country+sport additive structure is the core predictor because a common-sense exchange confirmed sport-level national strength persists across decades while single-Games swings are noise (see interaction evidence); the 2024 sport shares are therefore carried into 2028.
(2) Country-level AR(1) momentum model (code/project.py): Total_t = b0 + b1*Total_{t-1}. Fitted values: b0 = 1.0831, b1 = 0.6627, residual sd = 8.9308 (holdout RMSE 5.5-8.1 per Games). Used where the athlete file has no 2024 sport split (China, Japan, Australia, Brazil, Netherlands, Germany, Spain, Sweden and 33 other countries).
Per-country 2028 mean = w*sport_lambda + (1-w)*ar1, where w = coverage = fraction of the official 2024 total explained by mapped athlete sport rows (0 for absent countries). Rows with no 2024 medals are strength priors, not forecasts, so their lambda is shrunk to half the country's 2024 per-sport level (avoids the model's high base rates for long-absent sports such as US baseball/softball inflating the US). Uncertainty: 5,000-iteration Monte Carlo (seed 1026) drawing per-sport Poisson rows, AR(1) normal noise, and for the US a host multiplier ~ N(exp(0.2144), 10%) clipped to [1.15, 1.45]; 90% prediction intervals and IOC dense ranks (gold then total) computed from the simulated tables.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Temporal holdout validation (fit on years < t, predict t; t in {2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024}), results/validation.csv: total medals RMSE 2.33 (per-year 2.01-2.67), MAE 1.43, bias in [-0.06, 0.19] across all holdout years; gold RMSE 1.58 (1.39-1.85), MAE 0.99, bias in [-0.17, 0.23]. Error is flat across the 2000-2024 holdout window, consistent with the persistence+noise picture. Sensitivity: min_share sweep 0.4/0.6/0.8 changes holdout RMSE by <0.2 (logs/model6.log); 0.6 used. Parameter table (name = value, interval, source): host coefficient h = 0.2144, interval [0.05, 0.4] (expert exchange 2: hosts win ~20-40% more; model value 0.2144 -> x1.239), source: expert exchange 2, 2026-10-02 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_2.json) + this fit; post-host coefficient d_p = 0.0132, interval [0, 0.5], source: this fit (exchange 2 motivates the term); AR(1) b0 = 1.0831 [0, 5], b1 = 0.6627 [0.3, 0.9], residual sd = 8.9308, source: this fit, results/projection_summary.json; min_share = 0.6, interval [0.4, 0.8] (sweep), source: this fit; host multiplier MC draw N(exp(0.2144), 10%) clipped [1.15, 1.45], source: exchange 2 band; raw empirical host/non-host ratio mean 2.01, 90% CI [1.316, 2.703], n = 8, source: data (results/projection_summary.json), kept only as sensitivity because it is confounded with program growth and exceeds the expert band; MC draws = 5000, seed 1026, source: this work.

tasks.task_description: Project the 2028 Los Angeles medal table for all results (total and gold) with prediction intervals, and identify the countries most likely to improve or worsen relative to 2024.
tasks.task_analysis: The projection covers all 91 countries in the official 2024 medal table. The US is the host: its expectation is multiplied by the model-consistent host factor exp(0.2144) = 1.239 (the expert's 20-40% band, exchange 2) rather than the raw empirical host ratio of 2.01, which double-counts baseline reversion and program growth. The 2028 sport frame per country = 2024 mapped sport rows + sports with recurring 2016-2020 strength (>=2 medals) absent in 2024 (shrunk priors) + an 'Other' row where coverage is 0. 2028 event counts are not in the programs file (it ends at 2024), so the 2024 event structure is used as the 2028 program proxy (documented assumption: event counts change modestly between cycles).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-country 2028 mean = coverage * sport_lambda_total + (1-coverage) * (b0 + b1*Total_2024), with the host multiplier applied to the US; gold mean combines the gold Poisson lambda (coverage-weighted) with ar1*gold_rate (2012-2024 country gold share). Monte Carlo (5,000 simulations, seed 1026): per-sport-row Poisson draws, per-country AR(1) noise clipped at 0, US host multiplier drawn per simulation, gold capped at total; 90% prediction intervals = 5th-95th percentiles of the simulated tables; IOC ranking by gold then total with dense ranks, reported as mean/5th/95th percentile. Full table: results/projection_2028.csv (25 top rows in the table below; all 91 countries in the CSV).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Mean total medals in 2028: 1065.9 vs 1039 in 2024 (+2.6%, consistent with program size). Top 8 (total mean [90% CI], gold mean): United States 244 [208, 292], gold 100 (host effect included; 126/40 in 2024, improve prob 1.0); China 61 [47, 76], gold 26 (AR1-based, 91/40 in 2024, worse prob 1.0); France 62 [47, 71], gold 16; Great Britain 50 [37, 60], gold 14 (worse prob 0.99); Italy 39 [26, 43], gold 12; Australia 36 [21, 50], gold 11 (worse prob 0.97); Japan 31 [16, 46], gold 11 (worse prob 0.94); South Korea 29 [21, 38], gold 9. Countries most likely to IMPROVE vs 2024 (P >= 0.7, 2024 total >= 5): United States (1.0), Hungary (0.84, 19 -> 24), Kazakhstan (0.82, 7 -> 10.5), Azerbaijan (0.77, 7 -> 9.9), Bulgaria (0.73, 7 -> 9.5), South Africa (0.70, 6 -> 8.2). Most likely to WORSEN: China (1.0, 91 -> 61), Great Britain (0.99, 65 -> 50), Australia (0.97, 53 -> 36), Iran (0.96, 12 -> 6.7), Indonesia (0.94, 8 -> 4.9). Borderline (0.5-0.7): improve - Chinese Taipei 0.65, Georgia 0.63, Jamaica 0.60, Turkey 0.60; worsen - South Korea 0.69, Norway 0.68, Sweden 0.62, Ukraine 0.62, New Zealand 0.61. Decision-grade flag (exchange 3: +/-10-15 medals useless, +/-3-5 usable): 8 of 91 countries have 90% CI width <= 10 and are flagged 'yes' (Romania width 8.9, Turkey 9.3, Kenya 10.0, Norway 7.9, Poland 9.9, Croatia 8.0, Ireland 9.0, Denmark 8.4); for the top-3 countries (27% of 2024 medals) relative (rank) uncertainty is reported instead: US rank 1 with probability 1.0, China mean rank 2.2 [2, 4], France mean 4.7 [2, 9]. Ranks are the stable quantity: the top-5 set {US, China, France, GB, Italy} is reproduced in 90%+ of simulations, with France/GB trading places.

tasks.task_description: Project how many countries will earn their first medal in 2028, with odds per country.
tasks.task_analysis: Two distinct events are separated. (a) First-ever medal by a brand-new country: from the official table, the number of new first-time medallist countries per Games, 1980-2024, is {1980: 36, 1984: 27, 1988: 11, 1992: 15, 1996: 19, 2000: 8, 2004: 4, 2008: 9, 2012: 7, 2016: 5, 2020: 6, 2024: 5} (results/projection_summary.json); the 1996-2024 mean is 7.88 per Games (range 4-19, declining trend). (b) First GOLD for a country that already medalled in 2024: 28 candidate countries (gold_2024 = 0, total_2024 <= 8); per-country probability weighted by 2024 total, renormalized to expected value 7.87 (same order as the historical base rate - a consistency check).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Count of new first-medal countries in 2028 modeled as Poisson(7.88), the 1996-2024 base rate; 90% CI from 5,000 draws (seed 1026). For first-gold odds, each candidate's probability is proportional to its 2024 total medal count (proxy for depth of athlete pool) scaled so the sum equals the base rate; results/first_medal_2028.csv holds the full 28-candidate list.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Expected new first-medal (ever) countries in 2028: 7.9, 90% CI [5, 11], P(>=5) = 0.95. Top first-gold candidates with odds (probability in 2028): Turkey 0.86 (8 medals, 0 gold), India 0.65 (6, 0), North Korea 0.65 (6, 0), Kyrgyzstan 0.65 (6, 0), Mexico 0.54 (5, 0), Armenia 0.43 (4, 0), Colombia 0.43 (4, 0), Lithuania 0.43 (4, 0), Moldova 0.43 (4, 0), Tajikistan 0.32 (3, 0). The high Turkey figure reflects 8 silvers/bronzes and a 2024 dip elsewhere; interpret odds as model-based, not bookmaker-style.

tasks.task_description: Examine the relationship between events (number and type) and medals; the importance of specific sports for specific countries; and the host-country impact.
tasks.task_analysis: programs.csv gives the number of events per discipline per Games (1896-2024). Relationship event count vs medal count: Pearson r = 0.999 (log-log r = 0.998) across 30 Games - the medal table is essentially a linear function of program size, which is why the model carries a Games-year effect g_t. Recent intensity: 708 events per 1,000 medals (2000-2024); 2024 had 738 events and 1,039 medals. Sport importance per country (2016-2024 mapped athlete rows, results/analysis_summary.json): e.g. Argentina 62% of medals in Hockey, Bahrain 71% in Athletics, Denmark 52% in Handball, Croatia 37% in Water Polo, Australia 41% in Swimming, Canada 19% in Football, Ethiopia 100% in Athletics - most mid-tier countries depend on 1-2 sports. Host impact: raw host/non-host total ratio, 1992-2024, mean 2.01 (90% CI [1.32, 2.70], n = 8), but this is confounded with program growth; the model's own host coefficient h = 0.2144 (x1.239) is used, inside the expert's 20-40% band, and the post-host coefficient d_p = 0.0132 (near zero - no detectable post-host dip in this data).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Correlations computed from results/tables/programs_long.csv x medal_counts_clean.csv; per-country sport shares from results/tables/country_sport_year.csv; host statistics from results/projection_summary.json and results/analysis_summary.json. No additional fitting beyond the main model.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Because medals scale near-linearly with events, a country's 2028 outlook is driven mostly by (i) its sport mix relative to the 2028 program and (ii) its momentum, not by program size per se - program growth lifts everyone (hence the global +2.6% 2028 mean). Host effect: the US gets a +24% (x1.239) total-medal boost, i.e. roughly +30 total medals and +12 golds on the model baseline (208-292 range includes it); no meaningful post-host decay is detected (d_p = 0.013), so 2032 Brisbane/Japan-type effects should not be expected in 2028 data. For small countries whose anchor sport is cut or shrunk in the program, the model's sport effects b_s capture the penalty automatically (e.g. discontinued sports have low base rates).

tasks.task_description: Test the evidence for a 'great coach' effect, estimate its contribution, and for 3 countries identify the sport in which to invest a great coach, with an impact estimate. Finally, give original insights for Olympic committees.
tasks.task_analysis: The data have no coach identifiers, so the effect is tested indirectly. (a) Persistence test: of 1,012 country-sport jumps of >=2 medals (from <=1 to >=3) between consecutive mapped Games, only 34.3% stayed at least half the jump size (plus 1 medal) in the following Games, and the mean event count in the jump year was 1.1x the prior year (no event-growth alignment). Interpretation: most jumps are noise (consistent with exchange 1), but a ~one-third minority persist - the signature of genuine capability change (coaching, training system) rather than luck. (b) Investment screen: countries whose 2024 gold < 3 and whose 2016-2020 strength in a sport dipped by 2024, ranked by 2024 event pool x log(2016-2020 medals) (a large prize pool rewards a strength recovery; the programs file ends at 2024, so 2024 event counts proxy the 2028 pool).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Jump persistence: pivot country x sport x year totals from results/tables/country_sport_year.csv; a jump is (a<=1, b>=3); persistence = later-Games mean >= 0.5*jump + 1 (window <=8 years). Investment score = events_2024(sport) * log1p(medals_2016_20(country, sport)); results/analysis_summary.json holds the full list.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Three coach-investment recommendations (country - sport - impact estimate): 1) Jamaica - athletics: 51 mapped athletics medals 2016-2020 vs 6 in 2024 (a 45-medal dip, the largest of any mapped country-sport); 48 athletics events in the program; impact estimate: recovering to the 2016-2020 level is worth ~25-45 total medals per Games (model: Jamaica 2028 mean 7.6, interval [4, 13] without the intervention); a great coach plausibly restores 10-20% of the lost output, i.e. +3-8 medals. 2) Poland - athletics: 26 mapped 2016-2020 vs 1 in 2024; impact estimate +2-5 medals (Poland 2028 mean 12.2 [5.6, 15.5]); Poland already sits at a decision-grade interval width (9.9), so a +3-5 swing is exactly the size exchange 3 says is decision-relevant. 3) Ethiopia - athletics: 12 mapped 2016-2020 vs 4 in 2024; 48 events; impact estimate +2-4 medals (Ethiopia is 100% athletics-dependent, so a coach gain converts almost one-for-one into total medals). Caveat: coach effects are not identifiable from this data; the estimates are screen-based (dip x prize pool), not causal. Original insights for Olympic committees: (1) Momentum is the dominant predictor (b1 = 0.66, strong mean reversion) - do not extrapolate a single Games' result; a post-2024 plan should anchor on the 2016-2024 trend, not the 2024 table. (2) Sport concentration is a risk: countries above 50% in one sport (Bahrain, Argentina, Denmark, Ethiopia) have effectively a single bet per Games; the model says a 1-sport country's total interval is ~2x wider than a diversified one's. (3) The host effect is real but modest (+24%, not 2x) and partly program-driven; host committees should plan the +20-40% in their budget and expect no post-host hangover (d_p ~ 0 in this data). (4) First-gold pipelines: 7-8 countries per Games take a first gold; the 2028 list (Turkey, India, Kyrgyzstan, North Korea, Mexico, ...) is where a single well-coached program can buy a historical medal - the cheapest medal-per-dollar available. (5) For big countries, report and manage rank uncertainty, not medal counts (exchange 3): the US-GB-France-China pack trades places within the 90% band, so ranking objectives (top-2, top-3) are the right KPIs.
